<p><b>Venezuela</b> (<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˌ/: secondary stress follows">ˌ</span><span title="&#39;v&#39; in &#39;vie&#39;">v</span><span title="/ɛ/: &#39;e&#39; in &#39;dress&#39;">ɛ</span><span title="&#39;n&#39; in &#39;nigh&#39;">n</span><span title="/ə/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;about&#39;">ə</span><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;z&#39; in &#39;zoom&#39;">z</span><span title="&#39;w&#39; in &#39;wind&#39;">w</span><span title="/eɪ/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;face&#39;">eɪ</span><span title="&#39;l&#39; in &#39;lie&#39;">l</span><span title="/ə/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;about&#39;">ə</span></span>/</a></span></span> <a href="/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key" title="Help:Pronunciation respelling key"><i title="English pronunciation respelling"><span style="font-size:90%">VEN</span>-ə-<span style="font-size:90%">ZWAY</span>-lə</i></a>; <small>American Spanish:&#160;</small><span title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA" lang="es-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish" title="Help:IPA/Spanish">[beneˈswela]</a></span>&#32;<span data-nosnippet="" id="ooui-php-1" class="ext-phonos ext-phonos-PhonosButton noexcerpt ext-phonos-PhonosButton-emptylabel oo-ui-widget oo-ui-widget-enabled oo-ui-buttonElement oo-ui-buttonElement-frameless oo-ui-iconElement oo-ui-buttonWidget" data-ooui="{&quot;_&quot;:&quot;mw.Phonos.PhonosButton&quot;,&quot;href&quot;:&quot;\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/transcoded\/3\/37\/Venezuela.ogg\/Venezuela.ogg.mp3&quot;,&quot;rel&quot;:[&quot;nofollow&quot;],&quot;framed&quot;:false,&quot;icon&quot;:&quot;volumeUp&quot;,&quot;data&quot;:{&quot;ipa&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;text&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;lang&quot;:&quot;en&quot;,&quot;wikibase&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;file&quot;:&quot;Venezuela.ogg&quot;},&quot;classes&quot;:[&quot;ext-phonos&quot;,&quot;ext-phonos-PhonosButton&quot;,&quot;noexcerpt&quot;,&quot;ext-phonos-PhonosButton-emptylabel&quot;]}"><a role="button" tabindex="0" href="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/3/37/Venezuela.ogg/Venezuela.ogg.mp3" rel="nofollow" aria-label="Play audio" class="oo-ui-buttonElement-button"><span class="oo-ui-iconElement-icon oo-ui-icon-volumeUp"></span><span class="oo-ui-labelElement-label"></span><span class="oo-ui-indicatorElement-indicator oo-ui-indicatorElement-noIndicator"></span></a></span><sup class="ext-phonos-attribution noexcerpt"><a href="/wiki/File:Venezuela.ogg" title="File:Venezuela.ogg">i</a></sup>), officially the <b>Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela</b> (Spanish: <i lang="es">República Bolivariana de Venezuela</i>),<sup id="cite_ref-const_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-const-12">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup> is a country on the northern coast of <a href="/wiki/South_America" title="South America">South America</a>, consisting of a <a href="/wiki/Continent" title="Continent">continental</a> landmass and many <a href="/wiki/Federal_Dependencies_of_Venezuela" title="Federal Dependencies of Venezuela">islands and islets</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Caribbean_Sea" title="Caribbean Sea">Caribbean Sea</a>. It has a territorial extension of 916,445&#160;km<sup>2</sup> (353,841&#160;sq&#160;mi), and its population was estimated at 29 million in 2022.<sup id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup> The capital and largest urban agglomeration is the city of <a href="/wiki/Caracas" title="Caracas">Caracas</a>.
</p><p>The continental territory is bordered on the north by the <a href="/wiki/Caribbean_Sea" title="Caribbean Sea">Caribbean Sea</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean" title="Atlantic Ocean">Atlantic Ocean</a>, on the west by <a href="/wiki/Colombia" title="Colombia">Colombia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Brazil" title="Brazil">Brazil</a> on the south, <a href="/wiki/Trinidad_and_Tobago" title="Trinidad and Tobago">Trinidad and Tobago</a> to the north-east and on the east by <a href="/wiki/Guyana" title="Guyana">Guyana</a>. Venezuela is a <a href="/wiki/Presidential_republic" class="mw-redirect" title="Presidential republic">presidential republic</a> consisting of <a href="/wiki/States_of_Venezuela" title="States of Venezuela">23 states</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_Capital_District" class="mw-redirect" title="Venezuelan Capital District">Capital District</a> and <a href="/wiki/Federal_Dependencies_of_Venezuela" title="Federal Dependencies of Venezuela">federal dependencies</a> covering Venezuela's offshore islands. Venezuela is among the most urbanized countries in Latin America;<sup id="cite_ref-encartaSA_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-encartaSA-14">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-UNpopstats_15-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UNpopstats-15">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup> the vast majority of Venezuelans live in the cities of the north and in the capital.
</p><p>The territory of Venezuela was <a href="/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas" title="Spanish colonization of the Americas">colonized by Spain</a> in 1522 amid resistance from indigenous peoples. In 1811, it became one of the first Spanish-American territories to <a href="/wiki/First_Republic_of_Venezuela" title="First Republic of Venezuela">declare independence</a> from the Spanish and to form part of the first federal Republic of Colombia (<a href="/wiki/Gran_Colombia" title="Gran Colombia">Gran Colombia</a>). It separated as a full sovereign country in 1830. During the 19th century, Venezuela suffered political turmoil and autocracy, remaining dominated by regional <a href="/wiki/Caudillo" title="Caudillo">military dictators</a> until the mid-20th century. Since 1958, the country has had a series of democratic governments, as an exception where most of the region was ruled by military dictatorships, and the period was characterized by economic prosperity. Economic shocks in the <a href="/wiki/1980s_oil_glut" title="1980s oil glut">1980s</a> and 1990s led to major political crises and widespread social unrest, including the deadly <a href="/wiki/Caracazo" title="Caracazo">Caracazo</a> riots of 1989, <a href="/wiki/1992_Venezuelan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempts" class="mw-redirect" title="1992 Venezuelan coup d&#39;état attempts">two attempted coups in 1992</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Carlos_Andr%C3%A9s_P%C3%A9rez#Impeachment" title="Carlos Andrés Pérez">impeachment of a President</a> for embezzlement of public funds charges in 1993. The collapse in confidence in the existing parties saw the <a href="/wiki/1998_Venezuelan_presidential_election" title="1998 Venezuelan presidential election">1998 Venezuelan presidential election</a>, the catalyst for the <a href="/wiki/Bolivarian_Revolution" title="Bolivarian Revolution">Bolivarian Revolution</a>, which began with a <a href="/wiki/1999_Constituent_Assembly_of_Venezuela" class="mw-redirect" title="1999 Constituent Assembly of Venezuela">1999 Constituent Assembly</a>, where a new <a href="/wiki/Constitution_of_Venezuela" title="Constitution of Venezuela">Constitution of Venezuela</a> was imposed. The government's <a href="/wiki/Populist" class="mw-redirect" title="Populist">populist</a> <a href="/wiki/Social_welfare" class="mw-redirect" title="Social welfare">social welfare</a> policies were bolstered by soaring oil prices,<sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> temporarily increasing social spending,<sup id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup> and reducing <a href="/wiki/Economic_inequality" title="Economic inequality">economic inequality</a> and poverty in the early years of the regime.<sup id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup> However, poverty began to rapidly increase in the 2010s.<sup id="cite_ref-UN_19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UN-19">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/2013_Venezuelan_presidential_election" title="2013 Venezuelan presidential election">2013 Venezuelan presidential election</a> was widely disputed leading to <a href="/wiki/2013_Venezuelan_presidential_election_protests" title="2013 Venezuelan presidential election protests">widespread protest</a>, which triggered another nationwide <a href="/wiki/Crisis_in_Venezuela" title="Crisis in Venezuela">crisis</a> that continues to this day.<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> Venezuela has experienced <a href="/wiki/Democratic_backsliding" title="Democratic backsliding">democratic backsliding</a>, shifting into an <a href="/wiki/Authoritarianism" title="Authoritarianism">authoritarian state</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Isidoro_LosadaBitar_Deeb2022_22-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Isidoro_LosadaBitar_Deeb2022-22">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup> It <a href="/wiki/International_rankings_of_Venezuela" title="International rankings of Venezuela">ranks low</a> in international measurements of <a href="/wiki/Media_freedom_in_Venezuela" class="mw-redirect" title="Media freedom in Venezuela">freedom of the press</a> and <a href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_Venezuela" title="Human rights in Venezuela">civil liberties</a> and has high levels of <a href="/wiki/Corruption_in_Venezuela" title="Corruption in Venezuela">perceived corruption</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Human_Rights_Watch_2021_23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Human_Rights_Watch_2021-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Venezuela is a <a href="/wiki/Developing_country" title="Developing country">developing country</a> having the world's <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_by_proven_oil_reserves" title="List of countries by proven oil reserves">largest known oil reserves</a> and has been one of the world's leading <a href="/wiki/Oil_exporter" class="mw-redirect" title="Oil exporter">exporters of oil</a>. Previously, the country was an underdeveloped exporter of agricultural commodities such as coffee and <a href="/wiki/Cocoa_bean" title="Cocoa bean">cocoa</a>, but oil quickly came to dominate exports and government revenues. The excesses and poor policies of the incumbent government led to the collapse of Venezuela's entire economy.<sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ELPAISfeb2015_25-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ELPAISfeb2015-25">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> The country struggles with record <a href="/wiki/Hyperinflation" title="Hyperinflation">hyperinflation</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Shortages_in_Venezuela" title="Shortages in Venezuela">shortages of basic goods</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> unemployment,<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup> poverty,<sup id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> disease, high child mortality, <a href="/wiki/Malnutrition" title="Malnutrition">malnutrition</a>, severe crime and corruption. These factors have precipitated the <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_refugee_crisis" title="Venezuelan refugee crisis">Venezuelan refugee crisis</a> where more than seven million people have fled the country.<sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup> By 2017, Venezuela was declared to be in <a href="/wiki/Default_(finance)" title="Default (finance)">default</a> regarding debt payments by <a href="/wiki/Credit_rating_agency" title="Credit rating agency">credit rating agencies</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> The crisis in Venezuela has contributed to a rapidly deteriorating <a href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_Venezuela" title="Human rights in Venezuela">human rights situation</a>. Venezuela is a charter member of the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a> (UN), <a href="/wiki/Organization_of_American_States" title="Organization of American States">Organization of American States</a> (OAS), <a href="/wiki/Union_of_South_American_Nations" title="Union of South American Nations">Union of South American Nations</a> (UNASUR), <a href="/wiki/ALBA" title="ALBA">Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America</a> (ALBA), <a href="/wiki/Mercosur" title="Mercosur">Mercosur</a>, <a href="/wiki/Latin_American_Integration_Association" title="Latin American Integration Association">Latin American Integration Association</a> (LAIA) and <a href="/wiki/Organization_of_Ibero-American_States" title="Organization of Ibero-American States">Organization of Ibero-American States</a> (OEI).
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</span></h2>
<p>According to the most popular and accepted version, in 1499, an expedition led by <a href="/wiki/Alonso_de_Ojeda" title="Alonso de Ojeda">Alonso de Ojeda</a> visited the Venezuelan coast. The <a href="/wiki/Stilt_houses" class="mw-redirect" title="Stilt houses">stilt houses</a> in the area of <a href="/wiki/Lake_Maracaibo" title="Lake Maracaibo">Lake Maracaibo</a> reminded the Italian navigator, <a href="/wiki/Amerigo_Vespucci" title="Amerigo Vespucci">Amerigo Vespucci</a>, of the city of <a href="/wiki/Venice" title="Venice">Venice</a>, Italy, so he named the region <i>Veneziola</i>, or "Little Venice".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMassabié2008153_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMassabié2008153-34">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> The Spanish version of <i>Veneziola</i> is <i>Venezuela</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThomas2005189_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2005189-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Mart%C3%ADn_Fern%C3%A1ndez_de_Enciso" title="Martín Fernández de Enciso">Martín Fernández de Enciso</a>, a member of the Vespucci and Ojeda crew, gave a different account. In his work <i>Summa de geografía</i>, he states that the crew found <a href="/wiki/Indigenous_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Indigenous people">indigenous people</a> who called themselves the <i>Veneciuela.</i> Thus, the name "Venezuela" may have evolved from the native word.<sup id="cite_ref-ICH_1958_386_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ICH_1958_386-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Previously, the official name was <a href="/wiki/State_of_Venezuela" title="State of Venezuela"><i>Estado de Venezuela</i></a> (1830–1856), <i>República de Venezuela</i> (1856–1864), <a href="/wiki/United_States_of_Venezuela" title="United States of Venezuela"><i>Estados Unidos de Venezuela</i></a> (1864–1953), and again <a href="/wiki/Republic_of_Venezuela" title="Republic of Venezuela"><i>República de Venezuela</i></a> (1953–1999).
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="History">History</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/History_of_Venezuela" title="History of Venezuela">History of Venezuela</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Pre-Columbian_history">Pre-Columbian history</span></h3>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti">.mw-parser-output .tmulti .multiimageinner{display:flex;flex-direction:column}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow{display:flex;flex-direction:row;clear:left;flex-wrap:wrap;width:100%;box-sizing:border-box}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .tsingle{margin:1px;float:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .theader{clear:both;font-weight:bold;text-align:center;align-self:center;background-color:transparent;width:100%}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbcaption{background-color:transparent}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .text-align-left{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .text-align-right{text-align:right}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .text-align-center{text-align:center}@media all and (max-width:720px){.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbinner{width:100%!important;box-sizing:border-box;max-width:none!important;align-items:center}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow{justify-content:center}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .tsingle{float:none!important;max-width:100%!important;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .tsingle .thumbcaption{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow>.thumbcaption{text-align:center}}</style><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:204px;max-width:204px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:IdolosRoques.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/IdolosRoques.jpg/200px-IdolosRoques.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="92" href="/wiki/Cult_image" title="Cult image">Cult image</a> sculpted in ceramic, <a href="/wiki/Los_Roques_Archipelago" title="Los Roques Archipelago">Los Roques Archipelago</a>.</div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Petroglifo,_Parque_Waraira_Repano.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Petroglifo%2C_Parque_Waraira_Repano.jpg/200px-Petroglifo%2C_Parque_Waraira_Repano.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="113" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Petroglifo%2C_Parque_Waraira_Repano.jpg/300px-Petroglifo%2C_Parque_Waraira_Repano.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Petroglifo%2C_Parque_Waraira_Repano.jpg/400px-Petroglifo%2C_Parque_Waraira_Repano.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3264" data-file-height="1840" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Petroglyph" title="Petroglyph">Petroglyph</a> in the <a href="/wiki/El_%C3%81vila_National_Park" title="El Ávila National Park">Waraira Repano National Park</a>.</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>Evidence exists of human habitation in the area now known as Venezuela from about 15,000 years ago. Tools from this period have been found on the high <a href="/wiki/River_terraces_(tectonic%E2%80%93climatic_interaction)" title="River terraces (tectonic–climatic interaction)">riverine terraces</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Pedregal_River" title="Pedregal River">Rio Pedregal</a> in western Venezuela.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKipfer200091_37-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKipfer200091-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Late_Pleistocene" title="Late Pleistocene">Late Pleistocene</a> hunting artifacts, including spear tips, have been found at a similar series of sites in northwestern Venezuela known as "El Jobo"; according to <a href="/wiki/Radiocarbon_dating" title="Radiocarbon dating">radiocarbon dating</a>, these date from 13,000 to 7,000 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKipfer2000172_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKipfer2000172-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>It is not known how many people lived in Venezuela before the Spanish conquest; it has been estimated at one million.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> In addition to indigenous peoples known today, the population included historical groups such as the <a href="/wiki/Kalina_people" title="Kalina people">Kalina</a> (Caribs), <a href="/wiki/Auak%C3%A9_people" title="Auaké people">Auaké</a>, <a href="/wiki/Caquetio" title="Caquetio">Caquetio</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mariche" class="mw-redirect" title="Mariche">Mariche</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Timoto%E2%80%93Cuica_people" title="Timoto–Cuica people">Timoto–Cuicas</a>. The Timoto–Cuica culture was the most complex society in Pre-Columbian Venezuela, with pre-planned permanent villages, surrounded by irrigated, terraced fields.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMahoney89_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMahoney89-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup> Their houses were made primarily of stone and wood with thatched roofs. They were peaceful, for the most part, and depended on growing crops. Regional crops included potatoes and <a href="/wiki/Ulluco" class="mw-redirect" title="Ulluco">ullucos</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-art_41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-art-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> They left behind works of art, particularly anthropomorphic ceramics, but no major monuments. They spun vegetable fibers to weave into textiles and mats for housing. They are credited with having invented the <a href="/wiki/Arepa" title="Arepa">arepa</a>, a staple in <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_cuisine" title="Venezuelan cuisine">Venezuelan cuisine</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalas2004&#91;httpsbooksgooglecombooksid6-1QnKS6xG4CpgPA142_142&#93;_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalas2004[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid6-1QnKS6xG4CpgPA142_142]-42">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the conquest, the population dropped markedly, mainly through the spread of new infectious diseases from Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130_39-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> Two main north–south axes of pre-Columbian population were present, who cultivated maize in the west and <a href="/wiki/Manioc" class="mw-redirect" title="Manioc">manioc</a> in the east.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130_39-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> Large parts of the <i><a href="/wiki/Llanos" title="Llanos">llanos</a></i> were cultivated through a combination of <a href="/wiki/Slash_and_burn" class="mw-redirect" title="Slash and burn">slash and burn</a> and permanent settled agriculture.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130_39-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Colonization">Colonization</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas" title="Spanish colonization of the Americas">Spanish colonization of the Americas</a>, <a href="/wiki/German_colonization_of_the_Americas" title="German colonization of the Americas">German colonization of the Americas</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Colonial_Venezuela" title="Colonial Venezuela">Colonial Venezuela</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Musterung-Welser-Armada.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Musterung-Welser-Armada.png/220px-Musterung-Welser-Armada.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Musterung-Welser-Armada.png/330px-Musterung-Welser-Armada.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Musterung-Welser-Armada.png/440px-Musterung-Welser-Armada.png 2x" data-file-width="678" data-file-height="515" /></a><figcaption>The German <a href="/wiki/Welser" class="mw-redirect" title="Welser">Welser</a> Armada exploring Venezuela.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1498, during his third voyage to the Americas, <a href="/wiki/Christopher_Columbus" title="Christopher Columbus">Christopher Columbus</a> sailed near the <a href="/wiki/Orinoco_Delta" title="Orinoco Delta">Orinoco Delta</a> and landed in the <a href="/wiki/Gulf_of_Paria" title="Gulf of Paria">Gulf of Paria</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey1892103_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey1892103-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> Amazed by the great offshore current of freshwater which deflected his course eastward, Columbus expressed in a letter to Isabella and Ferdinand that he must have reached Heaven on Earth (terrestrial paradise):
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r996844942">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 40px}.mw-parser-output .templatequote .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;padding-left:1.6em;margin-top:0}</style><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>Great signs are these of the Terrestrial Paradise... for I have never read or heard of such a large quantity of fresh water being inside and in such close proximity to salt water; the very mild temperateness also corroborates this; and if the water of which I speak does not proceed from Paradise then it is an even greater marvel, because I do not believe such a large and deep river has ever been known to exist in this world.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEZamora1993Voyage_to_Paradise_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZamora1993Voyage_to_Paradise-44">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p><a href="/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas" title="Spanish colonization of the Americas">Spain's colonization of mainland Venezuela started in 1522</a>, establishing its first permanent South American settlement in the present-day<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Venezuela&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup> city of <a href="/wiki/Cuman%C3%A1" title="Cumaná">Cumaná</a>.
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="German_colonization">German colonization</span></h4>
<p>In the 16th century, the king of Spain granted a concession in Venezuela to the German <a href="/wiki/Welser" class="mw-redirect" title="Welser">Welser</a> family. <a href="/wiki/Klein-Venedig" title="Klein-Venedig">Klein-Venedig</a> <sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup> became the most extensive initiative in the <a href="/wiki/German_colonization_of_the_Americas" title="German colonization of the Americas">German colonization of the Americas</a> from 1528 to 1546. The <a href="/wiki/Welser" class="mw-redirect" title="Welser">Welser</a> family were bankers to the Habsburgs and financiers of Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, who was also King of Spain and had borrowed heavily from them to pay bribes for his <a href="/wiki/Imperial_election,_1519" class="mw-redirect" title="Imperial election, 1519">Imperial election</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1528, Charles V granted the Welsers the right to explore, rule and colonize the territory, as well as to seek the mythical golden town of <a href="/wiki/El_Dorado" title="El Dorado">El Dorado</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> The first expedition was led by <a href="/wiki/Ambrosius_Ehinger" title="Ambrosius Ehinger">Ambrosius Ehinger</a>, who established <a href="/wiki/Maracaibo" title="Maracaibo">Maracaibo</a> in 1529. After the deaths of first Ehinger (1533), then <a href="/wiki/Nikolaus_Federmann" title="Nikolaus Federmann">Nikolaus Federmann</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Georg_von_Speyer" title="Georg von Speyer">Georg von Speyer</a> (1540), <a href="/wiki/Philipp_von_Hutten" title="Philipp von Hutten">Philipp von Hutten</a> persisted in exploring of the interior. In absence of von Hutten from the capital of the province, the crown of Spain claimed the right to appoint a governor. On Hutten's return to the capital, <a href="/wiki/Santa_Ana_de_Coro" class="mw-redirect" title="Santa Ana de Coro">Santa Ana de Coro</a>, in 1546, the Spanish governor <a href="/wiki/Juan_de_Carvajal" title="Juan de Carvajal">Juan de Carvajal</a> had Hutten and <a href="/wiki/Bartholomeus_VI._Welser" title="Bartholomeus VI. Welser">Bartholomeus VI. Welser</a> executed. Subsequently, <a href="/wiki/Emperor_Charles_V" class="mw-redirect" title="Emperor Charles V">Charles V</a> revoked Welser's concession. The Welsers transported German miners to the colony, in addition to 4,000 African <a href="/wiki/Slaves" class="mw-redirect" title="Slaves">slaves</a> to plant <a href="/wiki/Sugar_cane" class="mw-redirect" title="Sugar cane">sugar cane</a> plantations. Many of the German colonists died from tropical diseases, to which they had no <a href="/wiki/Immunity_(medical)" title="Immunity (medical)">immunity</a>, or through frequent wars with the <a href="/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas" title="Indigenous peoples of the Americas">indigenous inhabitants</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Late_15th_century_to_early_17th_century">Late 15th century to early 17th century</span></h3>
<p>Native <i><a href="/wiki/Cacique" title="Cacique">caciques</a></i> (leaders) such as <a href="/wiki/Guaicaipuro" title="Guaicaipuro">Guaicaipuro</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;1530–1568</span>) and <a href="/wiki/Tamanaco" title="Tamanaco">Tamanaco</a> (died 1573) attempted to resist Spanish incursions, but the newcomers ultimately subdued them; Tamanaco was put to death by order of <a href="/wiki/Caracas" title="Caracas">Caracas</a>' founder, <a href="/wiki/Diego_de_Losada" title="Diego de Losada">Diego de Losada</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-UNE_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UNE-50">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the 16th century, during the Spanish colonization, indigenous peoples such as many of the <a href="/wiki/Mariches" class="mw-redirect" title="Mariches">Mariches</a>, themselves descendants of the Kalina, were converted to <a href="/wiki/Roman_Catholicism" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Catholicism">Roman Catholicism</a>. Some of the resisting tribes or leaders are commemorated in place names, including Caracas, <a href="/wiki/Chacao_Municipality" title="Chacao Municipality">Chacao</a> and <a href="/wiki/Los_Teques" title="Los Teques">Los Teques</a>. The early colonial settlements focused on the northern coast,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130_39-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWunder2003130-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> but in the mid-18th century, the Spanish pushed farther inland along the <a href="/wiki/Orinoco_River" class="mw-redirect" title="Orinoco River">Orinoco River</a>. Here, the <a href="/wiki/Ye%27kuana" title="Ye&#39;kuana">Ye'kuana</a> (then known as the Makiritare) organized serious resistance in 1775 and 1776.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGott2005203_51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGott2005203-51">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Spain's eastern Venezuelan settlements were incorporated into <a href="/wiki/New_Andalusia_Province" title="New Andalusia Province">New Andalusia Province</a>. Administered by the <a href="/wiki/Royal_Audiencia_of_Santo_Domingo" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal Audiencia of Santo Domingo">Royal Audiencia of Santo Domingo</a> from the early 16th century, most of Venezuela became part of the <a href="/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_New_Granada" title="Viceroyalty of New Granada">Viceroyalty of New Granada</a> in the early 18th century, and was then reorganized as an autonomous <a href="/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Venezuela" title="Captaincy General of Venezuela">Captaincy General</a> starting in 1777. The town of Caracas, founded in the central coastal region in 1567, was well-placed to become a key location, being near the coastal port of <a href="/wiki/La_Guaira" title="La Guaira">La Guaira</a> whilst itself being located in a valley in a mountain range, providing defensive strength against <a href="/wiki/Pirate" class="mw-redirect" title="Pirate">pirates</a> and a more fertile and healthy climate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEwell19844_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEwell19844-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Independence_and_19th_century">Independence and 19th century</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_War_of_Independence" title="Venezuelan War of Independence">Venezuelan War of Independence</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar_2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar_2.jpg/170px-Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar_2.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="222" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar_2.jpg/255px-Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar_2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar_2.jpg/340px-Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar_2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1525" data-file-height="1990" /></a><figcaption><i>El Libertador</i>, <a href="/wiki/Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar" title="Simón Bolívar">Simón Bolívar</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After a series of unsuccessful uprisings, Venezuela, under the leadership of <a href="/wiki/Francisco_de_Miranda" title="Francisco de Miranda">Francisco de Miranda</a>, a Venezuelan marshal who had fought in the <a href="/wiki/American_Revolution" title="American Revolution">American Revolution</a> and the <a href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French Revolution</a>, <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_Declaration_of_Independence" title="Venezuelan Declaration of Independence">declared independence</a> as the <a href="/wiki/First_Republic_of_Venezuela" title="First Republic of Venezuela">First Republic of Venezuela</a> on 5 July 1811.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> This began the <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_War_of_Independence" title="Venezuelan War of Independence">Venezuelan War of Independence</a>. A devastating <a href="/wiki/1812_Caracas_earthquake" title="1812 Caracas earthquake">earthquake that struck Caracas in 1812</a>, together with the rebellion of the Venezuelan <i><a href="/wiki/Llanero" title="Llanero">llaneros</a></i>, helped bring down the republic.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChasteen2001103_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChasteen2001103-54">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar" title="Simón Bolívar">Simón Bolívar</a>, new leader of the independentist forces, launched his <a href="/wiki/Admirable_Campaign" title="Admirable Campaign">Admirable Campaign</a> in 1813 from <a href="/wiki/United_Provinces_of_New_Granada" title="United Provinces of New Granada">New Granada</a>, retaking most of the territory and being proclaimed as <i>El Libertador</i> ("The Liberator"). A <a href="/wiki/Second_Republic_of_Venezuela" title="Second Republic of Venezuela">second Venezuelan republic</a> was proclaimed on 7 August 1813, but lasted only a few months before being crushed at the hands of <a href="/wiki/Royalist_(Spanish_American_independence)" title="Royalist (Spanish American independence)">royalist</a> caudillo <a href="/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Tom%C3%A1s_Boves" title="José Tomás Boves">José Tomás Boves</a> and his personal army of <i>llaneros</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The end of the <a href="/wiki/Peninsular_War" title="Peninsular War">French invasion</a> of homeland Spain in 1814 allowed the preparation of a large expeditionary force to the American provinces under general <a href="/wiki/Pablo_Morillo" title="Pablo Morillo">Pablo Morillo</a>, with the goal to regain the lost territory in Venezuela and New Granada. As the war reached a stalemate on 1817, Bolívar reestablished the <a href="/wiki/Third_Republic_of_Venezuela" title="Third Republic of Venezuela">Third Republic of Venezuela</a> on the territory still controlled by the patriots, mainly in the <a href="/wiki/Guayana_Province" title="Guayana Province">Guayana</a> and <a href="/wiki/Llanos" title="Llanos">Llanos</a> regions. This republic was short-lived as only two years later, during the <a href="/wiki/Congress_of_Angostura" title="Congress of Angostura">Congress of Angostura</a> of 1819, the union of Venezuela with New Granada was decreed to form the Republic of Colombia (historiographically <a href="/wiki/Gran_Colombia" title="Gran Colombia">Republic of Gran Colombia</a>). The war continued for some years, until full victory and <a href="/wiki/Sovereignty" title="Sovereignty">sovereignty</a> was attained after the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Carabobo" title="Battle of Carabobo">Battle of Carabobo</a> on 24 June 1821.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGregory199289–90_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGregory199289–90-56">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup> On 24 July 1823, <a href="/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Prudencio_Padilla" title="José Prudencio Padilla">José Prudencio Padilla</a> and <a href="/wiki/Rafael_Urdaneta" title="Rafael Urdaneta">Rafael Urdaneta</a> helped seal Venezuelan independence with their victory in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Maracaibo" title="Battle of Lake Maracaibo">Battle of Lake Maracaibo</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ciawfb_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ciawfb-57">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> New Granada's congress gave Bolívar control of the Granadian army; leading it, he liberated several countries and founded the Republic of Colombia (<a href="/wiki/Gran_Colombia" title="Gran Colombia">Gran Colombia</a>).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGregory199289–90_56-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGregory199289–90-56">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:19_de_abril.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/19_de_abril.jpg/220px-19_de_abril.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="139" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/19_de_abril.jpg/330px-19_de_abril.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/19_de_abril.jpg/440px-19_de_abril.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1260" data-file-height="795" /></a><figcaption><i>Revolution of 19 April 1810</i>, the beginning of Venezuela's independence, by <a href="/wiki/Mart%C3%ADn_Tovar_y_Tovar" title="Martín Tovar y Tovar">Martín Tovar y Tovar</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Sucre went on to liberate <a href="/wiki/Ecuador" title="Ecuador">Ecuador</a> and become the second president of <a href="/wiki/Bolivia" title="Bolivia">Bolivia</a>. Venezuela remained part of Gran Colombia until 1830, when a rebellion led by Páez allowed the proclamation of a newly independent Venezuela, on 22 September;<sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup> Páez became the first president of the new <a href="/wiki/State_of_Venezuela" title="State of Venezuela">State of Venezuela</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-59">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> Between one-quarter and one-third of Venezuela's population was lost during these two decades of warfare (including perhaps one-half of the <a href="/wiki/Venezuelans_of_European_descent" title="Venezuelans of European descent">Venezuelans of European descent</a>),<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup> which by 1830, was estimated at 800,000.<sup id="cite_ref-Caudillismo_61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Caudillismo-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The colors of the <a href="/wiki/Flag_of_Venezuela" title="Flag of Venezuela">Venezuelan flag</a> are yellow, blue, and red: the yellow stands for land wealth, the blue for the sea that separates Venezuela from Spain, and the red for the blood shed by the heroes of independence.<sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Slavery" title="Slavery">Slavery</a> in Venezuela was abolished in 1854.<sup id="cite_ref-Caudillismo_61-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Caudillismo-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> Much of Venezuela's 19th-century history was characterized by political turmoil and dictatorial rule, including the Independence leader José Antonio Páez, who gained the presidency three times and served a total of 11 years between 1830 and 1863. This culminated in the <a href="/wiki/Federal_War" title="Federal War">Federal War</a> (1859–1863). In the latter half of the century, <a href="/wiki/Antonio_Guzm%C3%A1n_Blanco" title="Antonio Guzmán Blanco">Antonio Guzmán Blanco</a>, another <i>caudillo</i>, served a total of 13 years between 1870 and 1887, with three other presidents interspersed.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Martin_Tovar_y_Tovar_02.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Martin_Tovar_y_Tovar_02.jpg/220px-Martin_Tovar_y_Tovar_02.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="148" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Martin_Tovar_y_Tovar_02.jpg/330px-Martin_Tovar_y_Tovar_02.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Martin_Tovar_y_Tovar_02.jpg/440px-Martin_Tovar_y_Tovar_02.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1455" data-file-height="980" /></a><figcaption>The signing of Venezuela's independence, by <a href="/wiki/Mart%C3%ADn_Tovar_y_Tovar" title="Martín Tovar y Tovar">Martín Tovar y Tovar</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1895, a longstanding dispute with Great Britain about the territory of Guayana Esequiba, which Britain claimed as part of <a href="/wiki/British_Guiana" title="British Guiana">British Guiana</a> and Venezuela saw as Venezuelan territory, erupted into the <a href="/wiki/Venezuela_Crisis_of_1895" class="mw-redirect" title="Venezuela Crisis of 1895">Venezuela Crisis of 1895</a>. The dispute became a diplomatic crisis when Venezuela's lobbyist, <a href="/wiki/William_Lindsay_Scruggs" title="William Lindsay Scruggs">William L. Scruggs</a>, sought to argue that British behavior over the issue violated the United States' <a href="/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine" title="Monroe Doctrine">Monroe Doctrine</a> of 1823, and used his influence in Washington, D.C., to pursue the matter. Then, U.S. president <a href="/wiki/Grover_Cleveland" title="Grover Cleveland">Grover Cleveland</a> adopted a broad interpretation of the doctrine that declared an American interest in any matter within the hemisphere.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEZakaria1999145–146_63-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZakaria1999145–146-63">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup> Britain ultimately accepted arbitration, but in negotiations over its terms was able to persuade the U.S. on many of the details. A tribunal convened in Paris in 1898 to decide the issue and in 1899 awarded the bulk of the disputed territory to British Guiana.<sup id="cite_ref-Humphreys_64-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Humphreys-64">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1899, <a href="/wiki/Cipriano_Castro" title="Cipriano Castro">Cipriano Castro</a>, assisted by his friend <a href="/wiki/Juan_Vicente_G%C3%B3mez" title="Juan Vicente Gómez">Juan Vicente Gómez</a>, seized power in Caracas, marching an army from his base in the Andean state of <a href="/wiki/T%C3%A1chira" title="Táchira">Táchira</a>. Castro defaulted on Venezuela's considerable foreign debts and declined to pay compensation to foreigners caught up in Venezuela's civil wars. This led to the <a href="/wiki/Venezuela_Crisis_of_1902%E2%80%931903" class="mw-redirect" title="Venezuela Crisis of 1902–1903">Venezuela Crisis of 1902–1903</a>, in which Britain, Germany and Italy imposed a naval blockade of several months before international arbitration at the new <a href="/wiki/Permanent_Court_of_Arbitration" title="Permanent Court of Arbitration">Permanent Court of Arbitration</a> was agreed. In 1908, <a href="/wiki/Dutch-Venezuela_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Dutch-Venezuela War">another dispute</a> broke out with the Netherlands, which was resolved when Castro left for medical treatment in Germany and was promptly overthrown by <a href="/wiki/Juan_Vicente_G%C3%B3mez" title="Juan Vicente Gómez">Juan Vicente Gómez</a> (1908–1935).
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="20th_century">20th century</span></h3>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1097763485">.mw-parser-output .ambox{border:1px solid #a2a9b1;border-left:10px solid #36c;background-color:#fbfbfb;box-sizing:border-box}.mw-parser-output <figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:State_flag_of_Venezuela_(1954%E2%80%932006).svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/State_flag_of_Venezuela_%281954%E2%80%932006%29.svg/220px-State_flag_of_Venezuela_%281954%E2%80%932006%29.svg.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/State_flag_of_Venezuela_%281954%E2%80%932006%29.svg/330px-State_flag_of_Venezuela_%281954%E2%80%932006%29.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/State_flag_of_Venezuela_%281954%E2%80%932006%29.svg/440px-State_flag_of_Venezuela_%281954%E2%80%932006%29.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="900" data-file-height="600" /></a><figcaption>Flag of Venezuela between 1954 and 2006</figcaption></figure>
<p>The discovery of massive <a href="/wiki/Oil_field" class="mw-redirect" title="Oil field">oil deposits</a> in Lake Maracaibo during World War I<sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup> proved to be pivotal for Venezuela and transformed the basis of its economy from a heavy dependence on agricultural exports. It prompted an economic boom that lasted into the 1980s; by 1935, Venezuela's per capita gross domestic product was Latin America's highest.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECrow1980616–617_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrow1980616–617-66">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> Gómez benefited handsomely from this, as corruption thrived, but at the same time, the new source of income helped him centralize the Venezuelan state and develop its authority.
</p><p>He remained the most powerful man in Venezuela until his death in 1935, although at times he ceded the presidency to others. The <i>gomecista</i> dictatorship (1935–1945) system largely continued under <a href="/wiki/Eleazar_L%C3%B3pez_Contreras" title="Eleazar López Contreras">Eleazar López Contreras</a>, but from 1941, under <a href="/wiki/Isa%C3%ADas_Medina_Angarita" title="Isaías Medina Angarita">Isaías Medina Angarita</a>, was relaxed.  Angarita granted a range of reforms, including the legalization of all political parties. After <a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a>, immigration from Southern Europe (mainly from Spain, <a href="/wiki/Italo-venezuelans" class="mw-redirect" title="Italo-venezuelans">Italy</a>, Portugal, and France) and poorer Latin American countries markedly diversified Venezuelan society.<sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt,_1961.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt%2C_1961.jpg/220px-R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt%2C_1961.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="210" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/86/R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt%2C_1961.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="244" data-file-height="233" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt" title="Rómulo Betancourt">Rómulo Betancourt</a> (president 1945–1948 / 1959–1964), one of the major democracy leaders of Venezuela.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1945, a civilian-military coup overthrew Medina Angarita and ushered in <a href="/wiki/El_Trienio_Adeco" title="El Trienio Adeco">a three-year period of democratic rule</a> (1945–1948) under the mass membership party <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Action_(Venezuela)" title="Democratic Action (Venezuela)">Democratic Action</a>, initially under <a href="/wiki/R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt" title="Rómulo Betancourt">Rómulo Betancourt</a>, until <a href="/wiki/R%C3%B3mulo_Gallegos" title="Rómulo Gallegos">Rómulo Gallegos</a> won the <a href="/wiki/1947_Venezuelan_presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="1947 Venezuelan presidential election">1947 Venezuelan presidential election</a> (generally believed to be the first free and fair elections in Venezuela).<sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> Gallegos governed until overthrown by a military junta led by the triumvirate <a href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Felipe_Llovera_P%C3%A1ez&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Luis Felipe Llovera Páez (page does not exist)">Luis Felipe Llovera Páez</a><span class="noprint" style="font-size:85%; font-style: normal;">&#160;&#91;<a href="https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Llovera_P%C3%A1ez" class="extiw" title="es:Luis Llovera Páez">es</a>&#93;</span>, <a href="/wiki/Marcos_P%C3%A9rez_Jim%C3%A9nez" title="Marcos Pérez Jiménez">Marcos Pérez Jiménez</a>, and Gallegos' Defense Minister, <a href="/wiki/Carlos_Delgado_Chalbaud" title="Carlos Delgado Chalbaud">Carlos Delgado Chalbaud</a>, in the <a href="/wiki/1948_Venezuelan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1948 Venezuelan coup d&#39;état">1948 Venezuelan <i>coup d'état</i></a>.
</p><p>The most powerful man in the military <i>junta</i> (1948–1958) was Pérez Jiménez (though Chalbaud was its titular president) and was suspected of being behind the death in office of Chalbaud, who died in a bungled kidnapping in 1950. When the junta unexpectedly lost the <a href="/wiki/1952_Venezuelan_presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="1952 Venezuelan presidential election">1952 presidential election</a>, it ignored the results and Pérez Jiménez was installed as president<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2021)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>The military dictator Pérez Jiménez was forced out on 23 January 1958.<sup id="cite_ref-ciawfb_57-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ciawfb-57">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> In an effort to consolidate a young democracy, the three major political parties (<a href="/wiki/Acci%C3%B3n_Democr%C3%A1tica" class="mw-redirect" title="Acción Democrática">Acción Democrática</a> (AD), <a href="/wiki/COPEI" class="mw-redirect" title="COPEI">COPEI</a> and <a href="/wiki/Uni%C3%B3n_Republicana_Democr%C3%A1tica" class="mw-redirect" title="Unión Republicana Democrática">Unión Republicana Democrática</a> (URD), with the notable exception of the <a href="/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Venezuela" title="Communist Party of Venezuela">Communist Party of Venezuela</a>), signed the <a href="/wiki/Puntofijo_Pact" title="Puntofijo Pact">Puntofijo Pact</a> power-sharing agreement. The two first parties would dominate the political landscape for four decades.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mesa_donde_se_firm%C3%B3_el_Pacto_de_Punto_Fijo.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Mesa_donde_se_firm%C3%B3_el_Pacto_de_Punto_Fijo.jpg/220px-Mesa_donde_se_firm%C3%B3_el_Pacto_de_Punto_Fijo.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="158" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Mesa_donde_se_firm%C3%B3_el_Pacto_de_Punto_Fijo.jpg/330px-Mesa_donde_se_firm%C3%B3_el_Pacto_de_Punto_Fijo.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Mesa_donde_se_firm%C3%B3_el_Pacto_de_Punto_Fijo.jpg/440px-Mesa_donde_se_firm%C3%B3_el_Pacto_de_Punto_Fijo.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1510" data-file-height="1086" /></a><figcaption>Table where the <a href="/wiki/Puntofijo_Pact" title="Puntofijo Pact">Puntofijo Pact</a> was signed on 31 October 1958</figcaption></figure><p>
During the presidencies of <a href="/wiki/R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt" title="Rómulo Betancourt">Rómulo Betancourt</a> (1959–1964, his second term) and <a href="/wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_Leoni" title="Raúl Leoni">Raúl Leoni</a> (1964–1969) in the 1960s, substantial guerilla movements occurred, including the <a href="/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_National_Liberation_(Venezuela)" title="Armed Forces of National Liberation (Venezuela)">Armed Forces of National Liberation</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Revolutionary_Left_Movement_(Venezuela)" title="Revolutionary Left Movement (Venezuela)">Revolutionary Left Movement</a>, which had split from AD in 1960. Most of these movements laid down their arms under <a href="/wiki/Rafael_Caldera" title="Rafael Caldera">Rafael Caldera</a>'s first presidency (1969–1974); Caldera had won the <a href="/wiki/1968_Venezuelan_presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="1968 Venezuelan presidential election">1968 election</a> for COPEI, being the first time a party other than Democratic Action took the presidency through a democratic election. The new democratic order had its antagonists. Betancourt <a href="/wiki/Assassination_attempt_of_R%C3%B3mulo_Betancourt" title="Assassination attempt of Rómulo Betancourt">suffered an attack</a> planned by the Dominican dictator <a href="/wiki/Rafael_Trujillo" title="Rafael Trujillo">Rafael Trujillo</a> in 1960, and the leftists excluded from the Pact initiated an armed insurgency by organizing themselves in the Armed Forces of National Liberation, sponsored by the Communist Party and Fidel Castro. In 1962 they tried to destabilize the military corps, with failed revolts in Carúpano and Puerto Cabello. At the same time, Betancourt promoted a foreign policy, the <a href="/wiki/Betancourt_Doctrine" title="Betancourt Doctrine">Betancourt Doctrine</a>, in which he only recognized elected governments by popular vote.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability" title="Wikipedia:Verifiability"><span title="Quotation needed from source to verify. (April 2018)">need quotation to verify</span></a></i>&#93;</sup></p><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Caracas_Sabana_Grande_1973.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Caracas_Sabana_Grande_1973.jpg/220px-Caracas_Sabana_Grande_1973.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Caracas_Sabana_Grande_1973.jpg/330px-Caracas_Sabana_Grande_1973.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Caracas_Sabana_Grande_1973.jpg/440px-Caracas_Sabana_Grande_1973.jpg 2x" data-file-width="590" data-file-height="393" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Sabana_Grande,_Caracas" title="Sabana Grande, Caracas">Sabana Grande</a> district, <a href="/wiki/Caracas" title="Caracas">Caracas</a> (1973)</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/1973_Venezuelan_presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="1973 Venezuelan presidential election">The election in 1973</a> of <a href="/wiki/Carlos_Andr%C3%A9s_P%C3%A9rez" title="Carlos Andrés Pérez">Carlos Andrés Pérez</a> coincided with an <a href="/wiki/1973_oil_crisis" title="1973 oil crisis">oil crisis</a>, in which Venezuela's income exploded as <a href="/wiki/Oil_prices" class="mw-redirect" title="Oil prices">oil prices</a> soared; oil industries were nationalized in 1976. This led to massive increases in public spending, but also increases in external debts, until the collapse of oil prices during the 1980s crippled the Venezuelan economy. As the government started to devalue the currency in February 1983 to face its financial obligations, Venezuelans' real standards of living fell dramatically. A number of failed economic policies and increasing corruption in government led to rising poverty and crime, worsening social indicators, and increased political instability.<sup id="cite_ref-Schuyler_2001_10_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Schuyler_2001_10-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Carlos_Andr%C3%A9s_P%C3%A9rez.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Carlos_Andr%C3%A9s_P%C3%A9rez.jpg/170px-Carlos_Andr%C3%A9s_P%C3%A9rez.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="213" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/08/Carlos_Andr%C3%A9s_P%C3%A9rez.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="240" data-file-height="300" /></a><figcaption>President <a href="/wiki/Carlos_Andr%C3%A9s_P%C3%A9rez" title="Carlos Andrés Pérez">Carlos Andrés Pérez</a> was <a href="/wiki/Impeachment" title="Impeachment">impeached</a> on corruption charges in 1993.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In the 1980s, the Presidential Commission for State Reform (COPRE) emerged as a mechanism of political innovation. Venezuela was preparing for the decentralization of its political system and the diversification of its economy, reducing the large size of the State. The COPRE operated as an innovation mechanism, also by incorporating issues into the political agenda that were generally excluded from public deliberation by the main actors of the Venezuelan democratic system. The most discussed topics were incorporated into the public agenda: decentralization, political participation, municipalization, judicial order reforms and the role of the State in a new economic strategy. The social reality of the country made the changes difficult to apply.<sup id="cite_ref-:32_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:32-71">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Economic crises in the 1980s and 1990s led to a political crisis. Hundreds of people were killed by Venezuelan security forces and the military in the <i><a href="/wiki/Caracazo" title="Caracazo">Caracazo</a></i> riots of 1989 during the presidency of Carlos Andrés Pérez (1989–1993, his second term) and after the implementation of economic austerity measures.<sup id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez" title="Hugo Chávez">Hugo Chávez</a>, who in 1982 had promised to depose the bipartisanship governments, used the growing anger at economic austerity measures to justify a <a href="/wiki/1992_Venezuelan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempts" class="mw-redirect" title="1992 Venezuelan coup d&#39;état attempts">coup d'état attempt in February 1992</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-Marquez124_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Marquez124-73">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BBCprofile_74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBCprofile-74">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> a <a href="/wiki/1992_Venezuelan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempts" class="mw-redirect" title="1992 Venezuelan coup d&#39;état attempts">second coup d'état attempt occurred in November</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-BBCprofile_74-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBCprofile-74">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> President Carlos Andrés Pérez (re-elected in 1988) was impeached under embezzlement charges in 1993, leading to the interim presidency of <a href="/wiki/Ram%C3%B3n_Jos%C3%A9_Vel%C3%A1squez" title="Ramón José Velásquez">Ramón José Velásquez</a> (1993–1994). Coup leader Chávez <a href="/wiki/Rafael_Caldera#Amnesty_to_the_1992_coup_participants" title="Rafael Caldera">was pardoned in March 1994</a> by president Rafael Caldera (1994–1999, his second term), with a clean slate and his political rights reinstated, allowing Chávez to win and maintain the presidency continuously from 1999 until his death in 2013. Chávez won the elections of 1998, 2000, 2006 and 2012 and the presidential referendum of 2004. The only gaps in his presidency occurred during the <a href="/wiki/2002_Venezuelan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt" class="mw-redirect" title="2002 Venezuelan coup d&#39;état attempt">two-day de facto government</a> of <a href="/wiki/Pedro_Carmona_Estanga" class="mw-redirect" title="Pedro Carmona Estanga">Pedro Carmona Estanga</a> in 2002 and when <a href="/wiki/Diosdado_Cabello_Rond%C3%B3n" class="mw-redirect" title="Diosdado Cabello Rondón">Diosdado Cabello Rondón</a> acted as interim president for a few hours.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (August 2021)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Bolivarian_government:_1999.E2.80.93present"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Bolivarian_government:_1999–present">Bolivarian government: 1999–present</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Bolivarian_Revolution" title="Bolivarian Revolution">Bolivarian Revolution</a> and <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez" class="mw-redirect" title="Presidency of Hugo Chávez">Presidency of Hugo Chávez</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Chavez_Kirch_Lula141597.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Chavez_Kirch_Lula141597.jpg/220px-Chavez_Kirch_Lula141597.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="111" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Chavez_Kirch_Lula141597.jpg/330px-Chavez_Kirch_Lula141597.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Chavez_Kirch_Lula141597.jpg/440px-Chavez_Kirch_Lula141597.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3506" data-file-height="1769" /></a><figcaption>Chávez with fellow South American presidents <a href="/wiki/N%C3%A9stor_Kirchner" title="Néstor Kirchner">Néstor Kirchner</a> of Argentina and <a href="/wiki/Luiz_In%C3%A1cio_Lula_da_Silva" title="Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva">Lula da Silva</a> of Brazil</figcaption></figure>
<p>A collapse in confidence in the existing parties led to <a href="/wiki/Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez" title="Hugo Chávez">Hugo Chávez</a> being elected president in 1998 and the subsequent launch of a "Bolivarian Revolution", beginning with a 1999 <a href="/wiki/Constituent_assembly" title="Constituent assembly">constituent assembly</a> to write a new Constitution of Venezuela. The Bolivarian Revolution refers to a <a href="/wiki/Left-wing_populism" title="Left-wing populism">left-wing populism</a> <a href="/wiki/Social_movement" title="Social movement">social movement</a> and political process in Venezuela led by Chávez, who founded the <a href="/wiki/Fifth_Republic_Movement" title="Fifth Republic Movement">Fifth Republic Movement</a> in 1997 and the <a href="/wiki/United_Socialist_Party_of_Venezuela" title="United Socialist Party of Venezuela">United Socialist Party of Venezuela</a> in 2007. The "Bolivarian Revolution" is named after <a href="/wiki/Sim%C3%B3n_Bol%C3%ADvar" title="Simón Bolívar">Simón Bolívar</a>. According to Chávez and other supporters, the "Bolivarian Revolution" seeks to build a mass movement to implement <a href="/wiki/Bolivarianism" title="Bolivarianism">Bolivarianism</a>—<a href="/wiki/Popular_democracy" title="Popular democracy">popular democracy</a>, economic independence, equitable distribution of revenues, and an end to political corruption—in Venezuela. They interpret Bolívar's ideas from a <a href="/wiki/Populism" title="Populism">populist</a> perspective, using <a href="/wiki/Socialism" title="Socialism">socialist</a> rhetoric. This led to formation of the <b>Fifth Republic of Venezuela</b> (<a href="/wiki/Spanish_language" title="Spanish language">Spanish</a>: <i lang="es">Quinta República de Venezuela</i>), commonly known as the <b>Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela</b> (<a href="/wiki/Spanish_language" title="Spanish language">Spanish</a>: <i lang="es">República Bolivariana de Venezuela</i>), that continues to the present day. Venezuela has been considered the Bolivarian Republic following the adoption of the new <a href="/wiki/Constitution_of_Venezuela" title="Constitution of Venezuela">Constitution of 1999</a>.
Since Chávez's election into office, Venezuela developed into a <a href="/wiki/Dominant-party_system" title="Dominant-party system">dominant-party system</a>, dominated by the <a href="/wiki/United_Socialist_Party_of_Venezuela" title="United Socialist Party of Venezuela">United Socialist Party of Venezuela</a>. In April 2002, Chávez was briefly ousted from power in the <a href="/wiki/2002_Venezuelan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt" class="mw-redirect" title="2002 Venezuelan coup d&#39;état attempt">2002 Venezuelan coup d'état attempt</a> following popular demonstrations by his opponents,<sup id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-75">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup> but Chavez returned to power after two days as a result of demonstrations by poor Chávez supporters in Caracas and actions by the military.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2004295_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2004295-76">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELópez_Maya200516_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELópez_Maya200516-77">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup> Chávez also remained in power after an all-out national strike that lasted <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_general_strike_of_2002%E2%80%932003" title="Venezuelan general strike of 2002–2003">from December 2002 to February 2003</a>, including a strike/lockout in the state oil company <a href="/wiki/PDVSA" title="PDVSA">PDVSA</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-78">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Capital_flight" title="Capital flight">Capital flight</a> before and during the strike led to the reimposition of <a href="/wiki/Foreign_exchange_controls" title="Foreign exchange controls">currency controls</a> (which had been abolished in 1989), managed by the <a href="/wiki/CADIVI" class="mw-redirect" title="CADIVI">CADIVI</a> agency. In the subsequent decade, the government was forced into several currency devaluations.<sup id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-81">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Economist_82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Economist-82">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Businessweek_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Businessweek-83">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> These devaluations have done little to improve the situation of the Venezuelan people who rely on imported products or locally produced products that depend on imported inputs while dollar-denominated oil sales account for the vast majority of Venezuela's exports.<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> According to Sebastian Boyd writing at <a href="/wiki/Bloomberg_News" title="Bloomberg News">Bloomberg News</a>, the profits of the oil industry have been lost to "social engineering" and corruption, instead of investments needed to maintain oil production.<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Chávez survived several further political tests, including an <a href="/wiki/2004_Venezuelan_recall_referendum" title="2004 Venezuelan recall referendum">August 2004 recall referendum</a>. He was elected for another term <a href="/wiki/2006_Venezuelan_presidential_election" title="2006 Venezuelan presidential election">in December 2006</a> and re-elected for a third term in October 2012. However, he was never sworn in for his third period, due to medical complications; he died on 5 March 2013.<sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup> The presidential election that took place on Sunday, 14 April 2013, was the first since Chávez took office in 1999 in which his name did not appear on the ballot.<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Self-published_sources" title="Wikipedia:Verifiability"><span title="The material near this tag may rely on a self-published source. (October 2022)">self-published source?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
Under the Bolivarian government, Venezuela went from being one of the richest countries in Latin America to one of the poorest.<sup id="cite_ref-RICHtoRAGS_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RICHtoRAGS-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Economic_policy_of_the_Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez_administration" title="Economic policy of the Hugo Chávez administration">Hugo Chávez's socioeconomic policies</a> of relying on oil sales and importing goods resulted in large amounts of debt, no change to <a href="/wiki/Corruption_in_Venezuela" title="Corruption in Venezuela">corruption in Venezuela</a> and culminated into the <a href="/wiki/Crisis_in_Venezuela" title="Crisis in Venezuela">crisis in Venezuela</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-RICHtoRAGS_88-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RICHtoRAGS-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> As a result of the crisis, the <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_refugee_crisis" title="Venezuelan refugee crisis">Venezuelan refugee crisis</a>, the largest emigration of people in Latin America's history,<sup id="cite_ref-WPfeb18_89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WPfeb18-89">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> occurred, with over 7 million Venezuelans – about 20% of the country's population – emigrating.<sup id="cite_ref-LPgracias_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LPgracias-90">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-WSJfeb18_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WSJfeb18-91">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> Chávez also initiated <a href="/wiki/Bolivarian_missions" title="Bolivarian missions">Bolivarian missions</a>, programs aimed at helping the poor.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="Nicol.C3.A1s_Maduro"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Nicolás_Maduro">Nicolás Maduro</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro" title="Presidency of Nicolás Maduro">Presidency of Nicolás Maduro</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Crisis_in_Venezuela" title="Crisis in Venezuela">Crisis in Venezuela</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Dilma_Rousseff_and_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro_at_48th_Mercosur_Summit_(2).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Dilma_Rousseff_and_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro_at_48th_Mercosur_Summit_%282%29.jpg/220px-Dilma_Rousseff_and_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro_at_48th_Mercosur_Summit_%282%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="160" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Dilma_Rousseff_and_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro_at_48th_Mercosur_Summit_%282%29.jpg/330px-Dilma_Rousseff_and_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro_at_48th_Mercosur_Summit_%282%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Dilma_Rousseff_and_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro_at_48th_Mercosur_Summit_%282%29.jpg/440px-Dilma_Rousseff_and_Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro_at_48th_Mercosur_Summit_%282%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3518" data-file-height="2558" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro" title="Nicolás Maduro">Nicolás Maduro</a> with Brazilian President <a href="/wiki/Dilma_Rousseff" title="Dilma Rousseff">Dilma Rousseff</a> at the 48th <a href="/wiki/Mercosur" title="Mercosur">Mercosur</a> Summit in Brazil in 2015.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Poverty and inflation began to increase into the 2010s.<sup id="cite_ref-UN_19-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UN-19">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro" title="Nicolás Maduro">Nicolás Maduro</a> was elected in 2013 after the death of Chavez. Chavez picked Maduro as his successor and appointed him vice president in 2013. Maduro was elected president in 2013 following Chavez's death.<sup id="cite_ref-Economist_82-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Economist-82">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Nicolás Maduro has been the <a href="/wiki/President_of_Venezuela" title="President of Venezuela">president of Venezuela</a> since 14 April 2013, when he won the <a href="/wiki/2013_Venezuelan_presidential_election" title="2013 Venezuelan presidential election">second presidential election after Chávez's death</a>, with 50.61% of the votes against the opposition's candidate <a href="/wiki/Henrique_Capriles_Radonski" class="mw-redirect" title="Henrique Capriles Radonski">Henrique Capriles Radonski</a>, who had 49.12% of the votes. The <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Unity_Roundtable" title="Democratic Unity Roundtable">Democratic Unity Roundtable</a> contested his election as fraud and as a violation of the constitution. An audit of 56% of the vote showed no discrepancies,<sup id="cite_ref-BBC12June_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC12June-95">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> and the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Venezuela" class="mw-redirect" title="Supreme Court of Venezuela">Supreme Court of Venezuela</a> ruled that under Venezuela's Constitution, Nicolás Maduro was the legitimate president.<sup id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup> Opposition leaders and some international media consider the government of Maduro to be a dictatorship.<sup id="cite_ref-reuters-maduro_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-reuters-maduro-97">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-hrw-maduro_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-hrw-maduro-98">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-wpo-maduro_99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wpo-maduro-99">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-nyt-maduro_100-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-nyt-maduro-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> Since February 2014, hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans have protested over high levels of criminal violence, corruption, hyperinflation, and chronic scarcity of basic goods due to policies of the federal government.<sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> Demonstrations and riots have resulted in over 40 fatalities in the unrest between Chavistas and opposition protesters<sup id="cite_ref-2014protests_106-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2014protests-106">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> and opposition leaders, including <a href="/wiki/Leopoldo_L%C3%B3pez" title="Leopoldo López">Leopoldo López</a> and <a href="/wiki/Antonio_Ledezma" title="Antonio Ledezma">Antonio Ledezma</a> were arrested.<sup id="cite_ref-2014protests_106-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2014protests-106">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-INDEPENDENT_108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-INDEPENDENT-108">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> Human rights groups condemned the arrest of <a href="/wiki/Leopoldo_L%C3%B3pez" title="Leopoldo López">Leopoldo López</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-112">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> In the <a href="/wiki/2015_Venezuelan_parliamentary_election" title="2015 Venezuelan parliamentary election">2015 Venezuelan parliamentary election</a>, the opposition gained a majority.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>Venezuela devalued its currency in February 2013 due to rising shortages in the country,<sup id="cite_ref-Businessweek_83-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Businessweek-83">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Shortages_in_Venezuela" title="Shortages in Venezuela">which included those of</a> milk, flour, and other necessities. This led to an increase in malnutrition, especially among children.<sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ECONeatCHAVISMO_116-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ECONeatCHAVISMO-116">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> Venezuela's economy had become strongly dependent on the exportation of oil, with crude accounting for 86% of exports,<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> and a high price per barrel to support social programs. Beginning in 2014 the <a href="/wiki/Price_of_oil" title="Price of oil">price of oil</a> plummeted from over $100/bbl to $40/bbl a year and a half later. This placed pressure on the Venezuelan economy, which was no longer able to afford vast social programs. To counter the decrease in oil prices, the Venezuelan Government began taking more money from <a href="/wiki/Petr%C3%B3leos_de_Venezuela,_S.A." class="mw-redirect" title="Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A.">PDVSA</a>, the state oil company, to meet budgets, resulting in a lack of reinvestment in fields and employees. Venezuela's oil production decreased from its height of nearly 3 to 1&#160;million <a href="/wiki/Barrel_(unit)#Oil_barrel" title="Barrel (unit)">barrels</a> (480 to 160&#160;thousand <a href="/wiki/Cubic_metre" title="Cubic metre">cubic metres</a>) per day.<sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-120">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup> In 2014, Venezuela entered an <a href="/wiki/Economic_recession" class="mw-redirect" title="Economic recession">economic recession</a>.<sup
